SwarmMind: Robots with Redundant Inference!

Community Article Published
November 23, 2026 Upvote 11 Ellia Cavanaugh ElliaC litert-community Bryce Hackel bhackel litert-community Darin Anthony Djapri DarinDjapri litert-community Kevin Hao kevinhaoaus123 litert-community
Team: Darin Djapri, Bryce Hackel, Ellia Cavanaugh, Kevin Hao

The problem

Running inference locally is essential in remote environments such as deep space, where robots cannot depend on cloud access. However, if the computer running the model fails mid-task, the robot may have to wait for it to reboot and restart inference. That interruption can disrupt critical tasks and create safety risks.
This is why we built a redundant local inference system that combines Gemma models running across different hardware with multiple camera inputs. When an inference machine fails, another resumes the model's unfinished response, preserving progress without cloud access or waiting for a reboot.

What we built: One mind, many bodies

(Also known as: A Leader-Elected Gemma Swarm with Mid-Sentence Handoff)

We connect heterogeneous devices over a local network into one fault-tolerant AI system. Each node runs Gemma 4 locally, while a priority-based leader election protocol selects the healthiest available machine to coordinate inference and robotic tasks.
Our key innovation is the mid-generation inference handoff. When a leader fails while generating a response, another node reconstructs the model's conversation context, including previously generated tokens, and resumes generation without restarting the answer.
As Gemma generates a response, the active node shares its output with the other machines, keeping them updated throughout inference. Each standby keeps its model loaded, so it can take over without a cold start. The system also shares camera inputs across the local network, allowing inference to run on a different machine from the one capturing the scene.
We demonstrate the architecture through a robotic laboratory assistant powered by a Seeed reBot arm and an AprilTag-calibrated overhead camera. This was designed to identify laboratory tools, detect hazards, infer experiments from visible equipment, identify missing items, and retrieve requested objects.

How we used LiteRT

SwarmMind supports Gemma 4 E4B across multiple inference backends and hardware platforms:

NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor: Gemma 4 E4B via Ollama, serving as the primary leader.
Lenovo Legion with RTX 4070: Gemma 4 E4B via Ollama, serving as a backup inference node and robotic hardware host.
Raspberry Pi 5: Gemma 4 E4B through LiteRT-LM, providing a resource-constrained inference backend.

Our LiteRT-LM integration supports explicitly prefilling the model's context with previously generated tokens, allowing inference to resume after another node fails.
Measured performance:

625 ms: Mid-generation handoff gap on real Gemma 4 E4B using Ollama, including a 600 ms failure-detection timeout.
0–60 ms: Leader election completion after detecting a failed peer.
1.5 ms: Median inter-node topic communication latency.

LiteRT-specific inference latency, memory usage, and power consumption have not yet been benchmarked separately.

What we learned

We began the project brainstorming various ideas, and initially settled on multi robot collaboration. We soon found out we were limited by: 1) Robots, 2) Wifi issues, 3) A broken gripper on the only robot we had. Looking back, that was the best thing that could have happened! Every dead link and flaky device was a live test of the exact problem we ended up solving. We stopped designing for the case where everything works and started designing for the case where nothing does. That's where rules like "never preempt a streaming job" and "truncate at the handoff" came from.
So, one of our biggest takeaways was that getting an AI model to produce a good answer is only one part of making an autonomous robot work. The system also has to manage asynchronous processes, network interruptions, hardware availability, and the timing of physical actions. We also learned how much the details of inference orchestration matter. A seemingly small decision, like when to synchronize generated tokens or when to declare a node unavailable, can determine whether a handoff is seamless or disruptive. We had to think carefully about failure-detection timeouts, communication overhead, generation boundaries, and the tradeoff between keeping standby models warm and conserving limited edge resources.
Most importantly, we learned that constraints can be productive. The problems that initially threatened to derail the project forced us to confront the assumptions hidden in conventional AI demos. A system that works only when every device is online, every connection is stable, and every process completes successfully isn't particularly autonomous. Building for failure made us build something much closer to what autonomy actually requires.

What's next: From robots that keep thinking to robots that keep learning

Right now, SwarmMind protects inference. The robots we're most excited about learn from experience. Methods like Real-Time EXPO-FT fine-tune vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning on real hardware. A large VLA proposes chunks of actions, a small edit policy adjusts them to the latest observation, and a Q-function picks the best one. For a robot like this, a crash costs much more. If its training machine dies, it loses its replay buffer, its in-progress weights and its optimizer state. That can mean hours of real-world experience that is slow and expensive to collect again.
So we want to extend SwarmMind from redundant inference to redundant learning. Experience would be copied across the swarm the same way tokens are today. Training state would be checkpointed and tagged by election term, so an outdated learner can't overwrite newer weights. If the learner fails, the next node loads the latest checkpoint and the copied experience and keeps training where the last one stopped. The split between a slow VLA and a fast edit policy also suits a mixed swarm: the VLA can run on the Thor and the edit policy on smaller edge devices. Our open questions include: how often to sync weights without saturating the network, and how to fail over from a large GPU to a smaller one without losing policy quality.
